newsitem.title: UK: Bosnian girl must stay with Britsh family - court. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bosnian girl must stay with Britsh family - court. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]

text.p: A four-year-old Bosnian girl, pulled from under her mother's body after a massacre, should stay with her British foster parents despite their "appalling irresponsibility" while adopting her, a British high court judge said on Monday.
(Corrects headline to read "Bosnian girl..." instead of "Serbian girl...".)
Sir Stephen Brown ruled that although her close relatives had traced Edita Keranovic and wanted her returned to their care, the girl's life should not be "shattered again".
Edita should therefore remain with the English family, the Fowlers, that had brought her to Britain for medical treatment and then adopted her.
"In my judgment her welfare requires that she should remain ... in the care of Mr and Mrs Fowler under the authority of the court," said Brown.
"However, it must fully and completely understood that she is not their daughter and that she is a Keranovic."

His statement to the court, given in private on Friday but made public on Monday, was translated line by line for Edita's relatives. They said later they were "very, very upset and disappointed with the decision that Edita should not return with us".
Edita's mother was machine-gunned to death by Bosnian Serb soldiers on May 31, 1992, the judge said, when they reached the village of Hrustovo.
The village's women and children had hidden in a garage but the soldiers had found them. They used machine guns and grenades to attack the garage.
"They perpetrated a massacre killing more than 30 women and children. Edita's mother and her brother Edin were killed as were her maternal grandmother, two aunts and two cousins," said Sir Stephen.
A Serbian officer apparently retrieved Edita, aged just nine weeks, from the pile of bodies and handed her to villagers. Edita had three pellets lodged in her brain and was taken to an orphanage.
Her plight was featured in British news reports and attracted the attention of Alan Fowler, 62, and his wife Deborah, 49. They arranged for Edita to be brought to Britain for medical treatment.

The couple were granted an adoption order even though, Brown said, they were aware Edita's grandfather was alive. They had given a "wholly inaccurate and misleading factual account of the circumstances in which Edita was found and of her origins".
But Brown said:"Her young life must not be shattered again." Edita will remain a ward of court, meaning judges will have control of her future.

"This situation requires sensitive and carful handling. I believe that Mr and Mrs Fowler, notwithstanding the appalling irresponsibility of their past behaviour are nevertheless capable of acting in Edita's interests."
Edita's grandfather Hasan Keranovic, said he wanted the child back."Edita is all that remains and we cannot be together. She is our child and belongs to us," he said.
